description:
Submit a tip! Tips@Midwest-Safety.com

Please consider JOINING for $1 a month. It *really* helps us do original reporting like this. 

CONTACT US:
Complaints? Video submissions? Sponsorships? Collabs? Business inquires? 
Email our board at mn.safety.alerts@gmail.com. 

BE NICE:
The individuals presented in these videos may be suffering from the effects of alcohol, drug abuse, a mental health disorder or simply having a bad day. The videos should NOT be presumed to be representative of their general behavior. Everyone deserves to be treated with respect. 

RIGHT TO BE FORGOTTEN:
Midwest Safety practices the "Right to be Forgotten." If you were the suspect in a lower-level offense, you may email our board to request removal. 
Email: mn.safety.alerts@gmail.com

The civilian footage appears to show the escorting officer just before the tractor trailer pulls away from the train, which may explain the initial confusion about the driver's location. The National Transportation Safety Board investigated the crash that caused the deaths of 63-year-old Claybird and 47-year-old Philip Arauio-Uho, the engineer and conductor. The NTSB examines every detail of derailments, especially catastrophic ones like this, which caused more than an estimated $6 million in damages. Three people inside the Chamber of Commerce sustained minor injuries, and about 9,000 gallons of diesel fuel leaked. Although many blamed the driver for stopping on the tracks, the ongoing investigation shows several serious factors that may have been the true cause. The front four locomotives completely derailed, and reports show one engine kept running after the crash. Chief Reeves stated in an investigative interview that officials were not trained on how to shut the engine down. 25 platform train cars also derailed. The report states that although the head-end locomotive had deflection plates, the semi-trailer was not pushed away, and the de methanizer tower instead rolled over the locomotive hood and into the windshield. The Federal Railroad Administration notes that studies show limited success for deflection plates, the severe impact, and the crushed cab area certainly caused the fatalities. The NTSB investigation notes this highway was a heavily used industrial corridor. Over 14,000 vehicles per day reportedly used this segment of US 285, and heavy truck activity reportedly represents 21% of that traffic. In the 10 years before the train crash, there were 89 car accidents in the 2,600 foot stretch of road around the crossing, Averaging about one crash every six weeks, three of those accidents were directly related to the railroad crossing. In the year before the crash, the crossing had seven incidents in which a driver broke the gate, including one involving a tractor trailer. The permit for this truck allowed a 145-foot, 198,000-pound vessel, far larger than a standard 18-wheeler, which is typically about 80 feet long and 80,000 pounds. The semi-truck was driven by a single driver for Boss Heavy Hall LLC. Notably, the company completed similar trips in the month before with no incidents. They held all required permits for the oversized load, used two escort vehicles, even requested a uniformed motorcycle officer, although police assistance was reportedly not required. 69 seconds before the crash, the trailer began to cross the tracks but was caught as the railroad signals activated, and the gate closed onto the vehicle. Expecting a low-grade railroad crossing, the driver tried to move forward, but the tires spun due to loss of friction. The vehicle was not bottoming out. It had enough clearance to cross. The driver engaged the differential lock to gain traction, but still could not move. With only seconds left, the driver abandoned the vehicle before the collision. From the train's perspective, no warning was provided, only until the crew could physically see the vehicle blocking the tracks. They applied the emergency brakes 11 seconds before impact, reducing speed from 68 miles per hour to 65. The speed limit on the track was 70 miles per hour, so speeding was no factor. The tractor driver, whose name we are withholding because of the ongoing investigation, had a valid commercial driver's license and a suspension-free record. The conductor and the engineer were also fully qualified and compliant. The NTSB ruled out intoxication, mechanical failure, and fatigue, and instead identified the core issue, the slope of the crossing. The tractor trailer was climbing a rise, pulling a long load over a crest, and fighting gravity. What appeared to be a flat Texas highway was, in reality, a trap for a vehicle of this size. In an interview with the president of Boss Heavy Hall, he explained that the escort or stearman operator could have restored traction by adjusting the trailer's height at individual axles using controls located outside the truck. However, he also stated that crossing the tracks should take two and a half to three minutes, far longer than the roughly 60 seconds of warning the railroad crossing allegedly provided. Another oversight involved the Texas Department of Motor Vehicles. Reportedly, the crossing had been designated as low ground clearance in 2019, yet no sign was present. Although the trailer never struck the tracks, such signs warned drivers that a crossing may take longer than usual and could have prompted added caution. Texas DMV also specifically approved this travel route for the vessel itself. An investigative interview confirmed that communication between the train and tractor companies is possible before a major railroad crossing. But the permit issued for the truck was for an oversized load, not a super load, so no advance communication was required. The key difference is wait. Any load exceeding roughly 250,000 pounds requires a super load permit and communication with train operators prior to crossing tracks. Beyond fixing the grade and updating policy, another solution is a vehicle detection system. Many rural railroad crossings lack any system to alert conductors to slow-moving or stopped vehicles on the tracks. Had the crew been warned that the gate was obstructed, they might have slowed enough to prevent fatalities. Fully stopping a train of that size would require at least a couple of minutes of warning and action. In the months following the incident, Union Pacific Railroad Company filed a lawsuit against Big Heavy Hall, the driver and several related logistics and gas companies. But court records show the case was dismissed. The docket does not state why, but it is possible there was a settlement. Union Pacific chose not to continue, or details from the NTSB report led them to drop the case. As of this posting, no criminal charges have been filed.

However, he also stated that crossing the tracks should take two and a half to three minutes,
far longer than the roughly 60 seconds of warning the railroad crossing allegedly provided.
Another oversight involved the Texas Department of Motor Vehicles.
Reportedly, the crossing had been designated as low ground clearance in 2019, yet no sign was present.
Although the trailer never struck the tracks, such signs warned drivers that a crossing may take longer than usual and could have prompted added caution.
Texas DMV also specifically approved this travel route for the vessel itself.
An investigative interview confirmed that communication between the train and tractor companies is possible before a major railroad crossing.
But the permit issued for the truck was for an oversized load, not a super load, so no advance communication was required.
The key difference is wait.
Any load exceeding roughly 250,000 pounds requires a super load permit and communication with train operators prior to crossing tracks.
Beyond fixing the grade and updating policy, another solution is a vehicle detection system.
Many rural railroad crossings lack any system to alert conductors to slow-moving or stopped vehicles on the tracks.
Had the crew been warned that the gate was obstructed, they might have slowed enough to prevent fatalities.
Fully stopping a train of that size would require at least a couple of minutes of warning and action.
In the months following the incident, Union Pacific Railroad Company filed a lawsuit against Big Heavy Hall,
the driver and several related logistics and gas companies.
But court records show the case was dismissed.
The docket does not state why, but it is possible there was a settlement.
Union Pacific chose not to continue, or details from the NTSB report led them to drop the case.
As of this posting, no criminal charges have been filed.
